title: Interfaces and type tests
body: An interface is a contract: a set of members that implementing types promise to provide. `interface IShape { double Area(); }` and `class Circle : IShape`. A type can implement many interfaces, which is how C# expresses 'can do' capabilities such as `IComparable<T>`, `IDisposable` and `IEnumerable<T>` without a shared base class.

Code written against an interface works with any implementation: a method taking `IShape` accepts circles, squares and test doubles. Depending on small interfaces rather than concrete classes makes code easier to test and change. Structs can implement interfaces too, but converting a struct to an interface type boxes it.

Explicit implementation (`double IShape.Area() => ...`) makes a member callable only through the interface, which resolves name clashes between two interfaces. Default interface methods (C# 8) give an interface member a body that implementers may override; use them to evolve published interfaces without breaking implementers. Static abstract members are covered with generic math in stage 7.

`is` tests a runtime type and can declare a variable (`if (shape is Circle c)`); `as` returns null instead of throwing when the cast fails; a direct cast `(Circle)shape` throws `InvalidCastException`. Prefer pattern-based `is` checks, and prefer virtual or interface members over long chains of type tests.

Before adding an interface, check that there are (or will be) multiple implementations or a testing seam; an interface for a single class adds indirection without benefit. Keep interfaces small and named for a capability.
